newsitem.title: PERU: Hostages spend Christmas under rebel guns in Peru.
newsitem.headline: Hostages spend Christmas under rebel guns in Peru.

text.p: More than a hundred tired and frightened VIP hostages spent Christmas Day under the guns of Marxist rebels holding the Japanese embassy residence, as Peru prayed for a softening of their captors' hearts.

While the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels refrained from repeating their "goodwill" releases of previous days, relatives and well-wishers flocked to the siege site hoping to bring the captives some Christmas cheer.
Blonde girls in miniskirts belted out carols through loudspeakers to the 105 hostages, cramped inside the compound for the eighth day.

A Jesuit priest who earlier turned down his chance of freedom led the mainly catholic hostages in prayer inside the compound. Throughout this Andean nation, Peruvians prayed for the release of the hostages.
They staged marches in provincial towns and hoisted flags from their homes. Family members sent seasonal messages over the airwaves to their loved ones.

"Brother, I'm sending you a huge hug ... God bless you, have faith like us, have hope that everything will end well," said Leonor Siura, the sister of captive Peruvian congressman Gilberto Siura, in a radio address.

The six mini-skirted girls, belonging to an American volunteer group called The Family, gave their impromptu concert from a scaffold erected next to police lines by the residence in the hope of cheering hostages' spirits.
Japanese media covering the siege hinted that a deal might be near to free the captives by allowing the Cuban-inspired rebels to take political exile in Havana.

The surprise release on Tuesday of Uruguayan ambassador Tabare Bocalandro following his country's freeing of two MRTA prisoners suggested behind-the-scenes, bilateral negotiations could be more energetic than the hardline, public stance of President Alberto Fujimori implied.
Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Badawi also left for Lima on Wednesday to intensify efforts to secure the release of Kuala Lumpur's ambassador to Peru, Ahmad Mokhtar.
The MRTA rebels stormed a smart reception at the residence on Tuesday night last week, taking prisoner about 500 VIPs from around the world.
Most -- including the old, the women, all the American and European hostages -- have now been released in what the rebels described as humanitarian gestures.

But the guerrillas were holding on to all the Peruvian government officials, including Fujimori's brother Pedro, the foreign minister and the head of the anti-terrorist police -- to press their demands for the release of jailed comrades.
Fujimori has rejected the conditions and told the guerrillas to surrender. But he insisted in a letter to Pope John Paul made public on Tuesday that he wanted a peaceful end to the crisis.

Peruvian crack troops were on alert to storm the fortified compound if needed as a last resort. Anti-terrorism police sources warned another MRTA unit was established in Lima, ready to strike other targets if the government turned to force.
Six ambassadors from Latin America and Asia, plus around 30 Japanese nationals, were among the remaining hostages.
"We can't celebrate Christmas knowing they are all in there," Tania Verdeguer, a friend of one of the hostages, told Reuters as she prayed for the captives near press lines.
Volunteers sent bibles for the Red Cross to take to the hostages along with Christmas meals that included traditional Japanese bento boxes -- packed lunches of fish and rice.

The hostages got a crumb of Christmas comfort when Peruvian police allowed the Red Cross to pump water into residence tanks to enable toilets to function for the first time since the mains supply was cut off last week.
Torches were also let into the residence to lessen the danger of an accident among the hostages during the nights of captivity, the Red Cross said.

Inside the residence, Jesuit priest Juan Julio Wicht was believed to have celebrated communion for the hostages. Red Cross workers were seen delivering candles and sacraments to the grand entrance of the residence on Tuesday evening.
Wicht turned down the chance of leaving the residence along with a group of 225 men set free on Sunday night, saying he preferred to stay and tend to his flock.
